title: Flushy vs the septic tank
caption: Flushy got launched out of the ground by a 4-ton tank. Here's how. 💩🚀
facts: Precast concrete septic tanks of about 1,000 gallons weigh roughly four to five tons (manufacturer specs).
Heavy solids settle as sludge; oils and grease rise as scum (US EPA).
T-shaped outlets keep sludge and scum from leaving the tank (US EPA).
Effluent seeps through drainfield gravel into soil, where soil microbes remove harmful bacteria and viruses (US EPA).
Wipes do not break down like toilet paper and build up in septic tanks (US EPA, wastewater utilities).
Pumping a tank while surrounding soil is saturated removes the liquid weight and can let groundwater float it (UF/IFAS Extension).

beats.text: Meet Flushy. A four-ton tank just launched him out of the ground.
Rewind. One flush earlier, Flushy is sliding down the pipe to his new home.
Welcome to the septic tank, where everyone gets sorted by weight. Heavy guys sink into the sludge. Greasy guys float up into the scum.
The exit has a bouncer: this T-pipe only lets the water in the middle out. Grease? Not tonight.
Outside, the water seeps through gravel, and billions of tiny soil microbes eat the germs. Free sewage treatment, right under your grass.
Then someone flushes wipes. Wipes don't break down. The gang grows, gunk escapes into the gravel, and the lawn becomes a stinky swamp.
So someone pumps the tank empty. During a flood. Empty, it's basically a concrete boat, and the rising groundwater shoves it straight up.
Flushy lands. In daylight. Ta-da. Next time: what your shower drain is hiding.
